records.sourceFile: Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy in Sports Musculoskeletal Injuries.pdf

paper.citation: Moghadam N, Hieda M, Ramey L, Levine BD, Guilliod R. Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy in Sports Musculoskeletal Injuries. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2019.
paper.abstract: The authors review the mechanisms, adverse effects and current evidence for hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) in sports musculoskeletal injuries. They conclude that human evidence is scarce and that HBOT should be tested in rigorous human trials before it is accepted as a way to speed return to play.
paper.tldr: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is popular with injured athletes, but human evidence is small and inconsistent, mostly on induced soreness. There are no human trials in muscle strain or contusion, so it should not be relied on to speed return to play.
paper.methods: Narrative review with no search method described. The authors discuss HBOT indications and mechanisms, adverse effects, and human trials in delayed-onset muscle soreness, muscle injury, and ligament and tendon injury, with animal and in vitro studies. They also review trial design limitations, including selection, performance and detection bias.
paper.findings: Eight human trials are summarised, including DOMS, ankle sprain, and medial collateral ligament injury studies with groups of about 6 to 16 participants. Some DOMS trials reported faster torque recovery or less pain with HBOT, but a prior systematic review reported higher pain at 48 and 72 hours with HBOT and no differences in longer-term pain, swelling or muscle strength. The authors found no human trials in muscle strain or contusion, and the ligament and tendon human studies were small and inconclusive. Half of the human trials used blinded outcome assessors. The authors conclude that the last systematic review and meta-analysis, which found HBOT ineffective for DOMS, still stands.
paper.limitations: The review has no described search, so selection of studies may be incomplete. Most human trials were small, with some lacking baseline comparisons, and sham designs used different pressures, which may weaken blinding. The authors note that basic and animal studies far outnumber human trials, and that these studies do not establish clinical benefit.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not use HBOT as an assumed way to speed recovery from muscle, ligament or tendon injury, since the human evidence is small and mixed. Before offering it, review the sham and blinding design of any trial you rely on, and monitor for barotrauma and oxygen toxicity (central nervous system and, with prolonged exposure, pulmonary), which the authors name as the two main concerns. Record outcomes carefully if you use it, given the uncertain benefit.
paper.athleteDev: The review addresses treatment of musculoskeletal injury and soreness, not training adaptation or performance enhancement, so it cannot inform performance programming.
paper.rtp: The authors state that rigorous human trials are needed before HBOT can be concluded to help athletes return to play. Current human evidence does not support using HBOT to set return-to-play timelines, and no clinical criteria are given.

records.sourceFile: Individuals with an ACL reconstructed knee display atypical whole body movement strategies but normal knee robustness during side-hop landings.pdf

paper.citation: Markström JL, Grip H, Schelin L, Häger CK. Individuals With an Anterior Cruciate Ligament-Reconstructed Knee Display Atypical Whole Body Movement Strategies but Normal Knee Robustness During Side-Hop Landings: A Finite Helical Axis Analysis. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;48(5):1117-1126.
paper.abstract: This controlled laboratory study compared landing control during standardized side-hop landings in 32 people with an ACL-reconstructed knee and 32 matched asymptomatic controls. Dynamic knee robustness was measured with a finite helical axis method, and whole-body movement strategies were compared with multivariate analyses. Knee robustness was similar between groups, but the reconstructed group used different trunk, hip and knee strategies and the reconstructed leg showed a knee flexor strength deficit.
paper.tldr: People with a reconstructed ACL landed differently from matched controls, with more hip and knee flexion at contact, even though knee robustness and most hop scores looked similar. Staff should consider whole-body landing strategy as well as limb symmetry when assessing these patients.
paper.methods: Controlled laboratory study with 32 people with an ACL-reconstructed knee and 32 matched asymptomatic controls. Participants performed standardized rebound side hops on force plates while motion capture recorded joint angles and moments, and knee robustness was measured with a finite helical axis approach. Groups and legs were compared with MANOVA, and one-leg hops and isometric knee strength were also recorded.
paper.findings: Knee robustness was lowest in the first 10 degrees of helical motion after initial contact and did not differ between groups or legs. Compared with controls, the reconstructed group had greater hip and knee flexion at initial contact (16 and 24 percent) and greater peak hip flexion, knee flexion and knee internal rotation moments, while the injured leg had greater trunk and hip flexion at contact and a 7 percent lower knee flexion moment than the noninjured leg. Hop distance was similar, the injured leg's one-leg vertical hop height was 8 percent lower than the noninjured leg, and knee flexor strength was 12 percent lower.
paper.limitations: The study is a single-session comparison, mainly recruited from one clinic, so causal links to reinjury cannot be drawn. Knee robustness was low in both groups right after landing, which the authors note is when injury risk is highest. The authors also note that the lack of knee abduction differences conflicts with earlier work and needs further research.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff could assess landing after ACL reconstruction using whole-body measures, such as trunk, hip and knee flexion at contact and knee moments, rather than relying only on limb symmetry in hop tests. Because knee robustness was low right after landing in both groups, the authors suggest training to improve control at initial contact, but this was not tested in the study.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not test performance outcomes. Its relevance to performance is that landing technique and whole-body control after reconstruction may matter for sport-specific side-hop tasks, which staff may consider when planning change-of-direction work.
paper.rtp: The study can inform return-to-sport assessment by showing that most hop and knee extensor measures met common symmetry criteria while the reconstructed group still used atypical landing strategies and had lower knee flexor strength. It cannot show that these strategies predict reinjury or that a particular test should clear athletes to return to sport.

records.sourceFile: Interrogating cortical representations in elite athletes with persistent posterior thigh pain - New targets for intervention.pdf

paper.citation: Summers SJ, Chalmers KJ, Wallwork SB, Leake HB, Moseley GL. Interrogating cortical representations in elite athletes with persistent posterior thigh pain - New targets for intervention? J Sci Med Sport 2021;24:135-140.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study compared tactile, proprioceptive and spatial processing in 14 male professional athletes with persistent posterior thigh pain after hamstring injury and 14 matched pain-free athletes. Patients were less accurate at localising touch on the affected leg and slower on left/right judgements of lower-limb images matching the affected leg, while two-point discrimination did not differ; auditory detection near the affected leg was lower on visual inspection but was not statistically tested. The authors conclude that leg-specific deficits exist and may contribute to persistent pain, which warrants further study.
paper.tldr: Elite athletes with persistent hamstring-related thigh pain showed leg-specific deficits in touch localisation and limb judgement on the affected side, with a possible, untested deficit in sound detection near that leg. The study cannot show that these deficits cause the pain to persist, so they are a reason to investigate, not a treatment target yet.
paper.methods: Fourteen male professional athletes with persistent posterior thigh pain after a grade 1 to 3 hamstring injury were compared with 14 pain-free athletes matched for age, sport, BMI and level, with data collected between 2007 and 2017 by a blinded examiner. Outcomes were two-point discrimination thresholds, tactile localisation error, left/right judgement response time for upper and lower limb images, and accuracy in detecting auditory clicks around each thigh. Groups were compared with independent t tests and legs with paired t tests (or non-parametric equivalents) under a prospectively published plan; the planned Wilcoxon test for the auditory task was not run, and an ultrasound post hoc test was added.
paper.findings: Two-point discrimination thresholds were similar between patients and controls (p = 0.70). Patients were less accurate at localising touch on the affected leg than on the unaffected leg (p = 0.004) or the matched leg of controls (p = 0.009), and slower on lower-limb left/right judgements when the image matched the affected leg than the unaffected leg (p = 0.001) or the matched leg of controls (p = 0.008); upper-limb judgements did not differ. Patients scored 86.4 +/- 17.6% on auditory detection for the affected leg and 100% for the unaffected leg, and controls scored 100% on both legs, but no test was reported because the lack of variance made the Wilcoxon test unsuitable.
paper.limitations: The sample is small and drawn from very elite athletes, so findings may not generalise to the wider athletic population. The tasks are indirect measures of cortical representation, no corrections were made for multiple comparisons, and the design cannot show whether deficits cause or follow persistent pain. The abstract reports p < 0.01 for the auditory task while the Results report no statistic for it. Ultrasound also showed grade 1 changes in 4 patients' unaffected legs and 4 controls, which the authors suggest may be false positives.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians treating persistent posterior thigh pain after hamstring injury may wish to assess touch localisation, limb judgement and sound detection as part of the picture, since leg-specific deficits were found in this group. Because the study cannot show that these deficits drive persistent pain, any training of cortical representations should be treated as untested in sport and monitored as such.
paper.athleteDev: This paper is about rehabilitation of a persistent injury, not performance development, so it has limited direct use for training prescription. It may be relevant to staff who work on movement and body awareness in athletes returning from hamstring injury.
paper.rtp: It can inform the question of why some hamstring injuries stay painful beyond expected recovery time, but it cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria or timelines. The study had no outcome data on recovery, re-injury or return to competition.

records.sourceFile: Kinematic and electromyographic analysis of the Askling L‐Protocol for hamstring training.pdf

paper.citation: Severini G, Holland D, Drumgoole A, Delahunt E, Ditroilo M. Kinematic and electromyographic analysis of the Askling L-Protocol for hamstring training. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2018;1-11.
paper.abstract: Eleven healthy individuals performed the three Askling L-Protocol exercises (extender, diver, glider) with EMG from four muscles and motion capture. The glider elicited peak hamstring activation of up to 60% MVC at a work point the authors liken to the running swing phase. Hamstring activation did not differ between the diver and glider, while the extender stretched the hamstrings with minimal engagement.
paper.tldr: The glider and diver exercises load the hamstrings at a joint position similar to the running swing phase, while the extender mainly stretches them. This describes muscle activity only and does not show how the protocol performs in rehabilitation.
paper.methods: Eleven participants did 10 repetitions of each exercise in random order. Surface EMG was recorded from biceps femoris, semitendinosus, rectus femoris and gluteus maximus, normalised to MVC tests, with motion capture of hip and knee angles. Root-mean-square EMG was compared across exercises, and muscle synergy analysis was used as a co-activation index.
paper.findings: In the glider, biceps femoris and semitendinosus peaked at 55 to 60% MVC at the start of the concentric phase, with eccentric-phase peaks reported as about 35% (Results) or 40% (Discussion). In the diver, hamstring peaks were below 50% MVC (about 40% in the Discussion) and gluteus maximus averaged about 48% MVC with peaks near 84%. The extender kept biceps femoris at a tonic 11.7% MVC with semitendinosus negligible, and hamstring RMS was significantly higher in the glider and diver than the extender, with biceps femoris higher in the glider than the diver during the eccentric phase.
paper.limitations: Eleven participants of mixed sex and activity level, EMG from the right leg only, and one session of 10 repetitions. The authors say the synergy analysis is not a neurophysiological measure, and eccentric-phase peak values differ between Results and Discussion. The study did not test strength, hypertrophy or return to sport.
paper.practicalImplications: The glider and diver produce submaximal hamstring activation during lengthening, lower than reported for the Nordic hamstring exercise (close to 100% MVC) and likely lower than in sprinting, with peaks as the hip begins to extend. The extender is mainly a flexibility exercise with low hamstring activation. Do not infer strength or injury-prevention effects from these EMG values.
paper.athleteDev: The glider and diver load the hamstrings at a joint position the authors liken to the running swing phase, but at lower activation than sprinting or the Nordic exercise. The extender is not a strength exercise in these data.
paper.rtp: The participants were healthy and uninjured, so the study cannot show how the L-Protocol performs in rehabilitation or set return-to-sport timing. The lower re-injury and shorter return to sport reported by Askling et al. were not tested here.
